passage: Sahil had it all on a sticky note by his hostel bed. The Wi-Fi dropped on the three nights before exams. The canteen ran out of paneer on the days fest meetings were called. The warden's scooter was parked at the admin block every time. "It's a plan," he told Dolma, his wingmate, eyes bright. "They want us distracted. Nobody else has noticed." He liked that part: the feeling of seeing what others missed. Dolma listened, then took out her own phone. "Let's test it. I'll note every Wi-Fi drop this month, exam or not." Three weeks later she showed him the list: eleven drops, only three near exams. Paneer ran out on random days. The warden's scooter was at admin almost daily. Sahil read it twice, a little deflated. "Huh. It looked so neat."

qa.q: How many Wi-Fi drops did Dolma note, and how many were near exams?
qa.a: Eleven drops, only three near exams.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel so pleased with his theory?
qa.a: The feeling of seeing what others missed; he felt special for having noticed a secret plan.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that made the "plan" testable?
qa.a: She noted every Wi-Fi drop for a month, exam or not, so the pattern could be compared with chance instead of a few hand-picked moments.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt listening to Sahil's bright-eyed theory?
qa.a: Dolma may have been doubtful but kind, choosing to test it together rather than mock it.

grounding: A hostel student strings unrelated events into a secret plan and feels special, until a wingmate tests it against a month of records.

Samir bhai,
You'll laugh, but I have to tell someone. For two weeks I've been seeing 17 everywhere. The bus I take is 17. My exam seat was 17. Our old hostel room was 17. I started thinking it meant something, like the universe was lining things up for me. Honestly, it felt amazing, like being let in on a secret.
Then I remembered your line: "What would it look like if it were just chance?" So yesterday I wrote down every number I noticed from morning to night. Forty-three numbers. Three were 17. I'd only remembered the 17s because I was hunting for them.
So, no cosmic message. Just my brain collecting hits and ignoring misses. Slightly sad, weirdly relieving. Come home soon. The bus is still 17.
Kunal

passage: Tenzin, it's Nirmala's confession time. Last semester I cracked a code, or thought I did. Professor Rao tells a lot of bad jokes in thermodynamics, right? passage: I'm Vikas, and I've shared a table with Sunaina in the college library since first year. This month she has a theory. The dance club's practice room lost power on three Fridays. The new CCTV camera went up outside it. The club's faculty adviser was on leave twice. "They're planning to shut us down," she told me, tapping her notebook where she'd drawn arrows between it all. "Nobody else sees it." Her eyes were bright; she seemed almost happy to be the one who'd noticed. I pointed out that the whole east wing lost power those Fridays, and the cameras went up across campus. She waved that off. "That's what they'd want us to think." I can't tell how much she really believes it. But she's added two more arrows since.

qa.q: How many Fridays did the practice room lose power?
qa.a: Three Fridays.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's bright-eyed excitement suggest about how the theory makes her feel?
qa.a: It suggests she feels special, like the only one clever enough to see a hidden plan.

qa.q: How could Sunaina test her theory instead of adding arrows?
qa.a: She could check whether other rooms lost power or got cameras too, and ask what she'd expect to see if it were all chance.

qa.q: How might the dance club's faculty adviser feel if they heard the theory?
qa.a: The adviser might be surprised or a little hurt to be cast as part of a plot for simply taking leave.

grounding: A classmate observes a young adult link unrelated events into a secret plan, pleased to have noticed it.

passage:
Monday. Elizabeth, twenty, was walking to her hostel in Kochi when the song her grandmother used to hum came on shuffle, just as she thought of her. She stopped under a streetlight, goosebumps rising.
Thursday. It had happened four more times. Elizabeth wrote each one in a notebook with the time. "It's a sign," she told Anjali at lunch, a little breathless. "Like she's telling me something. Nobody else would even notice."
Sunday. Anjali sat with her on the hostel steps. "Can I ask? How many times did the song play when you weren't thinking of her?" Elizabeth started to answer and stopped. She hadn't written those down. "And how often do you think of her?" "All the time," Elizabeth admitted. She looked at her notebook, and for the first time it seemed a bit thin.

qa.q: Where was Elizabeth walking when the song first played?
qa.a: To her hostel in Kochi.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she called it a sign?
qa.a: She felt moved and special, as if she alone had noticed a message meant for her.

qa.q: What question could help Elizabeth test the pattern, and why?
qa.a: Counting the times the song played when she wasn't thinking of her grandmother, since a real pattern should hold up against chance.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel asking questions about something so personal?
qa.a: Anjali probably feels careful and caring, wanting to help without hurting Elizabeth's feelings about her grandmother.

grounding: A young adult reads a secret meaning into coincidences and feels special, until a friend suggests testing it.

passage:
Irawati, you said just now that the universe is giving you signs about this college. Let me tell you about my signs.
I was twenty. I'd applied to a design school in Ahmedabad. That week I saw the number 7 everywhere: bus 7, room 7 in a hotel poster, seven crows on the wire. The school was on Road 7. I felt chosen, like I'd cracked a code nobody else could see. I told my friends it was destined.
My uncle, your grandfather's brother, asked, "How many times did you see 3, or 4? Did you count those?"
I hadn't. So for a week I wrote down every number I noticed. Pages of them. The 7s were no more than any other.
I didn't get in, by the way. I'm Vikas, and I got in the next year, with no crows involved.

qa.a: Writing down every number for a week was the turning point, because it tested the pattern and showed the 7s were no more common than other numbers.

qa.a: The uncle seemed calm and curious, treating it as something to test by counting other numbers too.

passage:
The scholarship results were out at six, the hostel corridor was full of drilling for the new water pipes, and Keerthana's phone read 11:11 again.
That made three times today. The bus that morning had been number 111. Her canteen token had said 11. She'd been born on the 11th.
"It's a message," she told Rukmini over the noise. "Things are lining up. I'm getting it."
Rukmini put down her book. "What did it mean when you saw 11:11 last month, before the debate?"
Keerthana paused. She'd lost the debate. "That was different."
"And the times you saw 11 and nothing happened?"
"I don't notice those."
"Exactly," Rukmini said, gently.
Keerthana looked at her phone. 11:12. Her stomach dropped. She'd felt so clever for noticing. Now it only felt like noticing.

qa.q: What number was the bus that morning?
How did Keerthana feel when the clock changed to 11:12?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt deflated and a little foolish, since the sense of a special message had gone.

qa.q: How could Keerthana test her 11 idea?
qa.a: She could note down every time she sees 11 and what happens afterwards, including the times nothing happens, and compare it with other numbers.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see the 11:11 signs?
qa.a: Rukmini sees them as coincidences that Keerthana notices only when they fit, and she asks questions to help her see it.

grounding: It shows a young adult linking chance numbers into a hidden message about a result, feeling special for noticing.

Jagdish had it all mapped out on a napkin in the college canteen. "Look. A white van outside the admin block three days in a row. The new phone tower on the library roof. The canteen shutting early. And the principal's been in Delhi twice this month."
Jasleen stirred her tea. "And?"
"They're selling the college. To some company. Nobody's noticed but me."
He was glowing. He hadn't felt this sharp all year.
"Okay," Jasleen said. "What would it look like if these things had nothing to do with each other?"
He opened his mouth.
"Vans deliver things. Towers go up everywhere. The canteen man's daughter is getting married, he told us."
"But the Delhi trips —"
"Could be ten reasons. How would you check?"
Jagdish looked at his napkin, the arrows suddenly thinner.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling while explaining his theory?

qa.q: Why was Jasleen's question a useful test?

Warden's note, boys' hostel. Nikita, resident warden.
Ojas, second year, came to me with a notebook today. Over two weeks he had linked the evening power cuts, the new mess contractor's van, two missing cycles and a changed Wi-Fi password into one story: someone was covering up thefts. He was excited, almost proud; he said nobody else had noticed.
I listened fully. Then we checked his notes against the electricity board's outage list: the cuts matched the whole area, not just our hostel. One cycle had been borrowed by a friend. The password change was my own doing. He looked deflated.
I thanked him for caring about hostel safety and suggested we log any new incidents together. I will check on him again next week.

Friday night

Something weird is going on at college. Omkar thinks I'm crazy, but listen. Three of my assignments got low marks this month. All three were checked on a Tuesday. The canteen stopped selling my favourite vada pav the same week. My name was spelled wrong on the notice board. Gautam

passage: In the market town of Karjat, Siddharth began noticing things. The bus was late on the days he wore his blue shirt. The shopkeeper Sudha gave him change in coins on the same days. The electricity went out twice when he was studying for his bank exam. 'It's connected,' he told Sudha one evening, leaning on her counter. 'Like something wants me to fail.' He felt a thrill saying it, as if he had seen behind a curtain. Sudha laughed. 'The bus is late for everybody, beta. And I give coins when I have no notes.' Siddharth frowned. 'But it fits.' 'Many things fit if you look only for fits,' she said, and handed him his tea. He walked home counting the blue-shirt days, and couldn't remember any others.
